items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The paper gives clear scope boundaries and future work but does not provide a systematic limitations or threats-to-validity discussion.
evidence: This paper aims to build on the work of the cited article to provide a detailed, easy-to-understand, and effective Model-Based Systems Engineering for those wishing to launch a CubeSat project, including the initial phases of preparation, management, and analysis, tailored for university projects carried out by cohorts of students.
The second part describes the MBSE Framework approach applied to the mission analysis phase of the MASAT1 Project.
The next step of this work is to improve the viability and practicality of the product breakdown structure model by integrating external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The academic nanosatellite context, MASAT1 mission, and lifecycle phases/reviews are described clearly, with the case application focused on mission analysis and early design.
evidence: MASAT1 is a nanosatellite project initiated at the University of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fez, Morocco to put in place the basic and indispensable technologies (hardware and software) necessary to build a resilient, ready-to-fly CubeSat system, with efficient power management and low-cost mission control ground station [21].
We have then summarized the cycle of a typical nanosatellite mission in 4 phases with deliverables reviews for each phase (Fig. 5):
Phase A of Mission Analysis results in a broad definition of the mission system, its functional and operational requirements, its architecture, and its constraints.

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The MASAT1 case provides illustrative model artifacts and traceability examples, but no quantitative metrics, baseline comparison, stakeholder evaluation, simulation output, integration/test, or flight evidence.
evidence: The proposed model-based approach is the result of experience gained from the MASAT1 project, a Moroccan university nanosatellite, and it is based on an architectural framework that allows the system to be described via a set of views.

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: The paper is a credible, highly relevant MBSE case/framework paper with clear academic nanosatellite context, SysML artifacts, lifecycle tailoring, and explicit requirements-to-design/verification traceability. Evidence is mainly conceptual and illustrative from MASAT1 rather than measured, executable, integrated, or flight-validated.

bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Retained as core because the full text directly proposes an MBSE/SysML framework for academic nanosatellite project management and design, applies it to MASAT1, and includes power-system/EPS-relevant structure, requirements, interface, and verification examples.
bibliographic_review_management.citation: Hanafi, A., Moutakki, Z., Karim, M., & Rachidi, T. (2024). Effective Model-Based Systems Engineering framework for academic nanosatellite project management and design. DOI: 10.1007/s12567-024-00542-2.
bibliographic_review_management.title: Effective Model-Based Systems Engineering framework for academic nanosatellite project management and design
bibliographic_review_management.publisher: Springer Nature / Council of European Aerospace Societies

RQ1.rationale: Directly addresses general nanosatellite mission modeling through an MBSE/SysML framework and includes EPS-relevant power-system requirements, components, interfaces, and behavior at early design abstraction. The limited-prior-knowledge aspect is implicit in the focus on first-time, limited-resource academic teams rather than experimentally tested.

RQ2.rationale: Claims improved reliability, traceability, consistency, reuse, communication, and management, with some EPS robustness requirements and interface models, but provides little measured evidence and only partial reproducibility/integrability evidence.

RQ3.rationale: Shows pre-physical model-level verification integration via SysML Verified By links, LEOP activity flow, and Bus System Activation state machine involving the power system, but does not report executable verification results, physical tests, or comprehensive EPS verification procedures.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: No comparison with prior extractions or other papers was performed under the silo rules. Within this paper, the authors position their framework relative to SSWG CubeSat MBSE, NASA MBSE strategy, and Guo et al.'s DelFFi nanosatellite MBSE work.

study_context_population.organization_type: University/academic project at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Fez, Morocco, with CNRST as main customer/funder.
study_context_population.project_maturity: First university nanosatellite project under development; paper emphasizes mission analysis and early design, with no flight or integration status reported.

study_context_population.model_maturity: SysML conceptual/early-design model with requirements, package, structural, interface, behavior, and verification traceability artifacts; executable SysML and external simulation integration are future work.

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Improve the success and early project management/design of university nanosatellite missions where traditional DBSE/ECSS practices are over-specified and academic teams have limited resources and experience.
modeling_scope: Academic nanosatellite lifecycle views and project timeline
Mission analysis view with needs definition, requirements definition, and functional breakdown processes
Product breakdown structure, work breakdown structure, and cost breakdown structure derivation
MASAT1 system requirements organization, requirement diagrams, tables, and matrices
Space and ground segment structural decomposition
Power-system block definition and internal block/interface diagrams
Concept of operations, LEOP activity flow, and bus activation state machine
Verification package and requirement Verified By links
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: Model boundary spans the nanosatellite project, space segment, payload, platform subsystems, ground segment, and selected subsystem/component detail; EPS is represented at component/interface level, not at circuit, electrochemical, or detailed power-budget simulation level.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: Business Agreement Structure is neglected for student projects; ECSS PBS is simplified; detailed executable simulation, MATLAB/STK integration, complete formal design, production/integration, operations, and physical test results are outside the reported work.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: Not quantified. The framework assumes basic familiarity with nanosatellite functions, stakeholder needs, requirements, ConOps, and ECSS/NASA systems-engineering concepts, while aiming to be understandable for first-time university CubeSat teams.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: The method starts from stakeholders, needs/goals/objectives, ConOps, and top-level requirements, then incrementally derives functions, product structure, interfaces, and behavior diagrams; reusable views and standards-derived categories reduce dependence on detailed prior behavior knowledge.
model_artifacts_used: Review deliverables such as MCR, MRR, SDR, PDR, CDR, SAR, PRR, ORR, and DR

implementation_pathway_tailoring.mapping_to_se_activities_lifecycle_gates: The framework maps Phase A Mission Analysis to needs definition, requirements definition, and functional breakdown with MCR/MRR/SDR-style reviews; Phase B Formal Design to preliminary design and PDR/CDR; Phase C Production & Integration to final design, integration, verification/acceptance, PRR/SAR; and Phase D Deployment & Operation to preparation, operations, ORR, and decommissioning review.
implementation_pathway_tailoring.approach_classification_rationale: The work is a SysML MBSE approach enhanced by tailoring ECSS/NASA project-management structures, lifecycle reviews, PBS/WBS/CBS governance, and academic-resource constraints; it is not yet an integrated digital-engineering environment because external analysis/simulation integration is future work.
tailoring_rationale: ECSS standards are considered over-specified for nanosatellite projects.
Academic nanosatellite projects are not typically customer-supplier relationships.
Functional requirements are mainly derived from mission objectives.
Budget is directly allocated to hardware acquisition and software development, so schedule and cost structures can be derived from the product tree.
Student personnel can change continuously, and Business Agreement Structure can be neglected.
Framework is intended for limited-resource teams wishing to start CubeSat/nanosatellite projects.

practical_implementation_pathway.rationale: The paper provides phase/process flows and applies them to MASAT1 with concrete SysML artifacts, though not an evaluated step-by-step deployment playbook.

toolchain_fragmentation_interoperability.rationale: The paper compares SysML tools, names MagicDraw/Cameo, describes SysML links/flows, and proposes MATLAB/STK integration, but provides no implemented exchange mechanism or continuity evidence.

lightweight_resource_constrained_tailori.rationale: The central framework tailors ECSS/NASA practices for limited-resource, student-driven academic nanosatellites and illustrates the tailoring in MASAT1.

governance_project_deliverables_roi_valu.rationale: PBS/WBS/CBS and review gates are central, but cost/schedule/ROI benefits are not measured.

newspace_agile_distributed_rapid_iterati.rationale: The paper mentions fast/cost-effective nanosatellites, iterative/recursive needs-requirements flows, and changing student personnel, but does not address agile, distributed, or rapid-iteration engineering practices in depth.

RQ1: A general academic nanosatellite model can be organized as SysML lifecycle/views and a PBS repository that starts with stakeholders, needs/goals/objectives, ConOps, top-level requirements, and functional breakdown.
EPS/power modeling is included at an early-design abstraction through 212 Power System requirements, Power System BDD components, power/data IBD interfaces, and bus activation behavior.

The approach reduces dependence on detailed prior behavior knowledge by giving first-time teams standards-derived process flows, package structures, and reusable requirement/product identifiers, but it does not prove minimal-knowledge usability empirically.
RQ2: The authors claim MBSE improves reliability, traceability, design consistency, communication, planning, management, development, and deliverable generation.
Reproducibility is supported conceptually by reusable packages and standards-derived structure, but no model repository/open assets are provided.
Integrability is supported by hardware/software BDDs and IBD data/power/service flows, but no integration test or flight evidence is reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated into the model through requirements tables/matrices with Satisfied By and Verified By columns.
The EPS-adjacent Power System satisfies mode-transition requirement 100.1.6, and the Bus System Activation state machine within the LEOP flow is given as the verification artifact.
The paper reports model-level verification linkage rather than executed simulations, verification coverage metrics, physical tests, or acceptance results.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The reported application is focused on the mission analysis phase and PBS development for MASAT1.
The authors state that executable SysML modeling is a future goal.
The next step is integration with external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK and development of a graphical user interface.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: No downloadable model, full requirements database, scripts, or open-source repository are reported.
No quantitative reliability, cost, schedule, communication, or reproducibility metrics are reported.
No executable simulation results, model checks, power-budget analysis, EPS test results, integration evidence, or flight/operations data are reported.
Venue name is not visible in the markdown, though DOI and publisher context are provided.
The EPS treatment is illustrative within a broader nanosatellite MBSE framework rather than a complete EPS-focused MBSE method.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This paper aims to contribute to research efforts to improve the success of university nanosatellite missions using Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) to facilitate the initial project management and design phases.

The proposed model-based approach is the result of experience gained from the MASAT1 project, a Moroccan university nanosatellite, and it is based on an architectural framework that allows the system to be described via a set of views.

However, with our limited resources, we encountered great difficulty in getting the project off to a good start, as most of the documentation and articles available cover the technical aspects of a CubeSat mission [11] and few articles detail the preparation and early phase management of a university nanosatellite mission.

The aim of using MBSE for a nanosatellite project is to create a model framework or repository that can be used by university teams (with limited resources) wishing to design CubeSat or Nanosatellite projects.
We used No Magic MagicDraw modeler with SysML and Cameo Simulation toolkit plugin.

The standard project breakdown method we just described works quite efficiently in an industrial customer-supplier relationship. However, some specificities of nanosatellite projects in an academic context allow for simplifying this structure model, since they are not in a customer-supplier relationship.

MASAT1 is a nanosatellite project initiated at the University of Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fez, Morocco to put in place the basic and indispensable technologies (hardware and software) necessary to build a resilient, ready-to-fly CubeSat system, with efficient power management and low-cost mission control ground station [21].
The system requirements for the MASAT1 mission are implemented in the MBSE model using the requirement diagrams and tables available in SysML.
These tables describe the requirements and their relationship to other SysML design elements to facilitate requirements traceability, satisfaction, and verification.
The "Satisfied By" column shows the model elements that fulfill the requirement. For example, the "Power System" subsystem must satisfy operational requirement 100.1.6.

The 'Verified By' column shows the specific test cases that determine how the system meets the requirement. For example, the "Bus System Activation" activity diagram (Fig. 23), which is part of the LEOP flow (Fig. 22), is used to verify operational requirement 100.1.6.
The SysML internal block diagrams (ibd) can be used to model connections between bdd internal components in terms of data, power, or service flow.

The LEOP flow activity diagram is also a way to "verify" functional or operational requirements, such as the Bus System Activation state machine (Fig. 23), which verifies operational requirements 100.1.6. that validate operational requirement 100.1.6.

To improve communication, planning, management, and development, we implemented this approach, replacing ad hoc procedures in the work organization with process flow and model based on the different views of the system architecture.
The next step of this work is to improve the viability and practicality of the product breakdown structure model by integrating external analysis and simulation tools such as MATLAB and STK.
